summary: At nearly 51 square miles, El Dorado Hills sprawls across the western Sierra Nevada foothills with a footprint larger than San Francisco's — yet holds barely 50,000 people, giving it a density of under 1,000 per square mile that reads more like rolling ranchland than suburb. That footprint means oak-studded ridgelines, seasonal creek drainages, and genuine elevation changes between subdivisions; evening light spills gold across west-facing slopes with views toward the Sacramento Valley floor. The tradeoff for all that space is a classic bedroom-community structure: no single dominant employer anchors the town, and the commute pattern flows heavily west on U.S. 50 toward Sacramento's government, healthcare, and tech offices roughly 25 miles away. A median home value of $870,300 against a median household income of $163,544 yields a price-to-income ratio around 5.3 — comfortable by California coastal standards, steep by almost anyone else's. The Town Center commercial area along El Dorado Hills Boulevard offers sit-down restaurants, chain grocers, and coffee shops, but the retail footprint thins quickly beyond it, reinforcing a car-dependent rhythm. With 9.3 hours of daily sunshine on average and mild winters, the trails threading through Folsom Lake State Recreation Area just to the north get year-round use. El Dorado Hills is essentially Sacramento's premium commuter shelf — spacious, sunny, and quiet, priced on the assumption that someone in the household drives to a paycheck somewhere else.
